The sum of the first $n$ bootstrap observations is the sum of $k$ complete selected block sums and, if $r>0$, the first $r$ entries of one additional selected block. Conditional on the data, these $k+\mathbf 1_{\{r>0\}}$ contributions are independent, and the centered covariance of each complete contribution is $C_b$, while that of the partial contribution is $C_r$ by uniformity of its start.

The covariance of a sum of independent centered Hilbert-valued random elements is the sum of their covariance operators: expanding the tensor product leaves only diagonal terms, since each off-diagonal expected tensor is the tensor of a zero mean with a zero mean. Dividing the sum by $n$ to obtain $\bar X_n^*$, and multiplying its covariance by $n$, gives $(kC_b+C_r)/n$.

**Input:** observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, an integer $1\le b\le n$, and a window $w:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ that vanishes off $[0,1]$, is positive on a neighbourhood of $1/2$, satisfies $w(1-u)=w(u)$, and is nondecreasing on $[0,1/2]$. Put $w_b(r)=w((r-\tfrac12)/b)$ for $1\le r\le b$, $W_b=(\sum_{r=1}^bw_b(r)^2)^{1/2}$, and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b$. The procedure is admissible only when $W_b>0$.

**Center and taper:** set $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and $R_t=Y_t-\bar Y_n$. For each start $j\in\{1,\ldots,n-b+1\}$, form the block

$$\bigl(a_bw_b(1)R_j,\ldots,a_bw_b(b)R_{j+b-1}\bigr).$$

**Resample:** use the independent uniform block starts from [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]], multiply each selected centered observation by its within-block taper and the factor $a_b$, concatenate in draw order, and retain the first $n$ entries. The conditional bootstrap mean is centered by its own conditional expectation when used to approximate the sampling law of $\sqrt n\,\bar Y_n$.

The factor $a_b$ compensates for the window's squared-weight sum in the block-sum variance calculation; this definition alone gives no bootstrap validity result.

For a dependent time series, the selected length-$b$ consecutive run is the resampling unit under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]]. The taper changes each unit record's within-block weight but the whole block is selected and resampled together; validity remains a separate theorem.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be monotone, that is
nondecreasing or nonincreasing on $[a,b]$ ([[def-monotone-function]]). Then $f$
is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$
([[def-darboux-integral]]).

Moreover, for the uniform partition $U_N$ of $[a,b]$ into $N \ge 1$ parts
([[def-partition-and-refinement]]),

$$U(f,U_N) - L(f,U_N) \;=\; \bigl|f(b) - f(a)\bigr| \cdot \frac{b-a}{\iota(N)} ,$$

where $\iota(N)$ is the canonical natural of $N$ in $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-canonical-natural]]). The right-hand side is an **equality**, not an
estimate: the sum $\sum_{i<N}(M_i - m_i)$ telescopes exactly, because on each
subinterval a monotone function attains its extremes at the two endpoints.

No continuity is assumed, and none holds in general: a nondecreasing function may
be discontinuous at every rational
([[thm-monotone-with-prescribed-discontinuity-set]]), and the companion page of
this pair works out the integral of the floor function, the simplest
discontinuous monotone integrand.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then $f$ is Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$
([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if**

$$\text{for every real } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ there is a partition } P \text{ of } [a,b] \text{ with } U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$$

([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

**This is the criterion every later integrability proof on this page uses.** It
replaces a statement about a supremum and an infimum over all partitions, which
cannot be checked directly, by the exhibition of a **single** partition for each
$\varepsilon$. The criterion says nothing about the value of the integral; that
separate lower-and-upper-sum estimate places the integral between $L(f,P)$ and
$U(f,P)$ for the same $P$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and let $I \in \mathbb{R}$. The following are equivalent.

1. **(Darboux)** $f$ is Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$ with
   $\int_a^b f = I$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).
2. **(Riemann)** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$
   such that
   $$\bigl|\,S(f,P,\xi) - I\,\bigr| \;<\; \varepsilon$$
   for **every** tagged partition $(P,\xi)$ of $[a,b]$ with $\|P\| < \delta$
   ([[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], [[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

**The quantifier over tagged partitions is universal, and that is the content.**
Condition 2 constrains every tagged partition of small mesh at once, tags
included; it is not a statement about one sequence of tagged partitions, and it
cannot be weakened to one. The companion page of this pair exhibits a
non-integrable function whose Riemann sums are constant along such a sequence.

**Boundedness is a hypothesis of both conditions as stated here.** Condition 1
presupposes it, since the Darboux sums of an unbounded function do not exist
([[def-darboux-sums]]); condition 2 makes sense for unbounded $f$ as well, and
in fact implies boundedness, but that implication is not proved here and is not
used: every application on this page starts from a bounded $f$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be **bounded**
([[def-bounded-set]]), so that there is a real $M \ge 0$ with $|f(x)| \le M$ for
every $x \in [a,b]$, and let $P = (n,t)$ be a partition of $[a,b]$ with
subintervals $I_i = [t_i, t_{i+1}]$ and lengths $\Delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i$ for
$i < n$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

### The two extreme values on a subinterval

For $i < n$ put

$$m_i \;:=\; \inf f[I_i], \qquad M_i \;:=\; \sup f[I_i], \qquad f[I_i] \;=\; \{\, f(x) : x \in I_i \,\} .$$

**Both exist.** The set $f[I_i]$ is nonempty, because $t_i < t_{i+1}$ makes $I_i$
nonempty ([[def-interval]]), and it is bounded, because $|f(x)| \le M$ for every
$x$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). A nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]); each is unique, so the notations
$\inf f[I_i]$ and $\sup f[I_i]$ name single real numbers ([[lem-sup-unique]]).

**They bracket the values, and each other.** For $x \in I_i$,

$$-M \;\le\; m_i \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M_i \;\le\; M ,$$

the outer inequalities because $-M$ is a lower bound and $M$ an upper bound of
$f[I_i]$, and the middle ones by the definitions of infimum and supremum. In
particular $m_i \le M_i$ and $M_i - m_i \le 2M$.

The dependence of $m_i$ and $M_i$ on $f$ and on $P$ is suppressed in the
notation, as is customary; where two partitions are in play the sums below carry
the partition and the extreme values are written out.

### The two Darboux sums

$$L(f,P) \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} m_i \,\Delta_i, \qquad U(f,P) \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} M_i \,\Delta_i ,$$

the finite sums of [[def-finite-sum]], indexed by $i \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$i < n$. Both are real numbers, being finite sums of reals, and

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

by monotonicity of finite sums, clause 4 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], since
$m_i \Delta_i \le M_i \Delta_i$ for every $i < n$: multiplying $m_i \le M_i$ by
$\Delta_i > 0$ preserves the inequality ([[def-ordered-field]]).

### The gap on a subinterval is the oscillation there

For every $i < n$,

$$M_i - m_i \;=\; \omega_f(I_i) \;=\; \sup\{\, |f(x) - f(y)| \ : \ x, y \in I_i \,\} ,$$

the oscillation of $f$ on the set $I_i$ ([[def-oscillation]]). The supremum is a
real number here rather than an extended one, because $f$ is bounded
([[def-oscillation]], [[def-extended-reals]]). The identity is proved in two
inequalities.

*The oscillation is at most the gap.* For $x, y \in I_i$ both $f(x)$ and $f(y)$
lie in $[m_i, M_i]$, so $f(x) - f(y) \le M_i - m_i$ and
$f(y) - f(x) \le M_i - m_i$, whence $|f(x) - f(y)| \le M_i - m_i$
([[lem-of-abs-value]]). So $M_i - m_i$ is an upper bound of the set whose
supremum is $\omega_f(I_i)$.

*The gap is at most the oscillation.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be real. By the
$\varepsilon$-characterisations of the supremum and the infimum
([[lem-sup-epsilon]], [[lem-inf-epsilon]]) there are $x, y \in I_i$ with
$f(x) > M_i - \varepsilon/2$ and $f(y) < m_i + \varepsilon/2$; then

$$|f(x) - f(y)| \;\ge\; f(x) - f(y) \;>\; (M_i - m_i) - \varepsilon ,$$

so $\omega_f(I_i) > (M_i - m_i) - \varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon > 0$ was
arbitrary, $\omega_f(I_i) \ge M_i - m_i$: otherwise
$\varepsilon := (M_i - m_i) - \omega_f(I_i)$ would be positive and give
$\omega_f(I_i) > \omega_f(I_i)$.

This identity is what connects the Darboux machinery to the pointwise
oscillation of [[def-oscillation]], and it is the hinge of
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

write $\mathbb E_B$ for a Bochner integral, and define $x\otimes y:H\to H$ by
$(x\otimes y)h=\langle h,y\rangle_Hx$. The Bochner series
$$ \Gamma=\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_0]+ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\bigl(\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j] +\mathbb E_B[X_j\otimes X_0]\bigr) $$
converges absolutely in trace norm to a positive self-adjoint trace-class
operator. For $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$, the Bochner covariance operators
$\Gamma_n=n^{-1}\mathbb E_B[S_n\otimes S_n]$ satisfy
$\|\Gamma_n-\Gamma\|_1\to0$. If $\boxtimes$ is the product-kernel class from
[[lem-real-l-two-kernel-operator-is-bounded-and-rank-one-compatible]], then
$$ \kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_0\boxtimes X_j],\qquad \widetilde\kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_j\boxtimes X_0] $$
are well-defined elements of $K=L^2([0,1]^2,dt\times dt;\mathbb R)$, and
$$ c=\kappa_0+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(\kappa_j+\widetilde\kappa_j) $$
converges absolutely in $K$ and satisfies $T_c=\Gamma$. Equivalently, $c$ is
the design's long-run covariance-kernel series interpreted as an
$L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class; no pointwise representatives are fixed.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space and let $(e_k)$ be a finite or countable
orthonormal family whose finite linear span is dense in $H$. Here
orthonormal means $\langle e_j,e_k\rangle_H=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise;
density means every $x\in H$ is arbitrarily close in norm to a finite linear
combination of the $e_k$. For $x\in H$, define
$$P_Nx=\sum_{k\le N}\langle x,e_k\rangle_H e_k,$$
using all basis vectors once $N$ reaches the size of a finite family. Then
$P_Nx\to x$ in norm and
$$\|x\|_H^2=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k\le N}|\langle x,e_k\rangle_H|^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a
compact self-adjoint operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Then $T$ has a
Hilbert basis ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]])
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]): one may take the union
of orthonormal bases of the finitely many-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces with a
Hilbert basis of $\ker T$. If $\ker T=\{0\}$ no vectors from the kernel are
needed, and if all nonzero eigenspaces are absent (that is $T=0$) the union is a
Hilbert basis of $H=\ker T$.

**Input:** observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, and $1\le b\le n$.

**Output:** a pseudo-series $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$, generated by [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]]: within each selected block retain the original order and concatenate blocks in their draw order, truncating only the last block when $b\nmid n$. The conditional bootstrap sample mean is $\bar X_n^*=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nX_t^*$. Its conditional center is $E^*\bar X_n^*$, where $E^*$ averages over the independent uniform block starts while the observations remain fixed.

This algorithm specifies the resampling law only. It does not assert that the conditional law approximates the sampling law for any data-generating process or block-length regime.

For a dependent time series, each selected length-$b$ run is treated as a predeclared group of consecutive unit records under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]]; the group is resampled intact and its within-block order is preserved. This is the sampling-unit interface, not a bootstrap-validity result.

**Input:** observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ in a real Hilbert space $H$, an integer $1\le b\le n$, and a window $w:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ that vanishes off $[0,1]$, is positive on a neighbourhood of $1/2$, satisfies $w(1-u)=w(u)$, and is nondecreasing on $[0,1/2]$. Put $w_b(r)=w((r-\tfrac12)/b)$ for $1\le r\le b$, $W_b=(\sum_{r=1}^bw_b(r)^2)^{1/2}$, and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b$. The procedure is admissible only when $W_b>0$.

**Center and taper:** set $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and $R_t=Y_t-\bar Y_n$. For each start $j\in\{1,\ldots,n-b+1\}$, form the block

$$\bigl(a_bw_b(1)R_j,\ldots,a_bw_b(b)R_{j+b-1}\bigr).$$

**Resample:** use the independent uniform block starts from [[alg-overlapping-block-resampling]], multiply each selected centered observation by its within-block taper and the factor $a_b$, concatenate in draw order, and retain the first $n$ entries. The conditional bootstrap mean is centered by its own conditional expectation when used to approximate the sampling law of $\sqrt n\,\bar Y_n$.

The factor $a_b$ compensates for the window's squared-weight sum in the block-sum variance calculation; this definition alone gives no bootstrap validity result.

For a dependent time series, the selected length-$b$ consecutive run is the resampling unit under [[def-resampling-sampling-unit-contract]]. The taper changes each unit record's within-block weight but the whole block is selected and resampled together; validity remains a separate theorem.

Let $w$ satisfy the taper conditions in [[alg-tapered-block-bootstrap]]. As the positive integer $b\to\infty$, $w^2$ is Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$, and

$$\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^b w\!\left(\frac{j-\tfrac12}{b}\right)^2\longrightarrow I_w:=\int_0^1 w(u)^2\,du>0.$$

Consequently, $W_b>0$ for all sufficiently large $b$ and $a_b=\sqrt b/W_b\to I_w^{-1/2}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $h\ge1$, $X_{h,h}$ is independent of $X_0$: its retained original innovation indices are $1,\ldots,h$, and its replacement array is independent of all inputs to $X_0$. Its mean is zero. Thus $E[X_0\otimes X_{h,h}]=0$ and $\|E[X_0\otimes X_h]\|_1\le\sigma\delta_h$ by [F3]–[F4]. For every finite real coefficient sequence $(u_t)$, expansion and $2|u_tu_{t+h}|\le u_t^2+u_{t+h}^2$ therefore give $E\|\sum_tu_tX_t\|^2\le K\sum_tu_t^2$. This proves the prefix bound. The same argument after applying $R=I-P$ gives $|E\langle RX_0,RX_h\rangle|\le\alpha_P\delta_h$, since $\|R\|\le1$ and projection preserves independence and centering. It proves the asserted projected prefix bound. Along complete basis projections, $\alpha_{P_d}\to0$ by norm convergence and dominated convergence, with dominating squared norm $\|X_0\|^2$.

Minkowski's inequality in $L^2(H)$ and the finite-coefficient bound in step 1.1 give $\|N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NX_{j+\ell-1}\|_{L^2(H)}\le\sqrt{K/N}$ for each $\ell$. Hence $\|\bar Z_{n,b}\|_{L^2(H)}\le b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^b|c_{b,\ell}|\sqrt{K/N}\le A\sqrt{Kb/N}$, as claimed. Minkowski here follows by expanding a finite squared norm and applying Cauchy–Schwarz to each cross term.

Put $D_{t,m}=X_t-X_{t,m}$. For $h\ge1$, $X_{h,h}$ is independent of $D_{0,m}$, so $|E\langle D_{0,m},X_h\rangle|\le\delta_m\delta_h$. If $h\ge m$, $X_{h,m}$ is independent of $D_{0,m}$, while for $1\le h<m$, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds $|E\langle D_{0,m},X_{h,m}\rangle|$ by $\delta_m\sigma$. Consequently the individual lag bounds are $|E\langle D_{0,m},D_{h,m}\rangle|\le\delta_m(\delta_h+\sigma)$ for $h<m$ and $\le\delta_m\delta_h$ for $h\ge m$. Negative-lag scalar covariances equal their positive counterparts by stationarity. Expanding any bounded-weight block and bounding each $|c_{b,\ell}c_{b,\ell+h}|$ by $A^2$ gives $\sup_{j,b}E\|b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^bc_{b,\ell}D_{j+\ell-1,m}\|^2\le A^2\varepsilon_m^2$, where $\varepsilon_m^2=\delta_m^2+2\delta_m\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h+2\sigma(m-1)\delta_m\to0$. The convergence uses precisely the assumed $m\delta_m\to0$ and summability.

Fix $m$. Write $Y_t=X_{t,m}$ and define $V_t=Y_t\mathbf1_{\{\|Y_t\|\le M\}}-E[Y_0\mathbf1_{\{\|Y_0\|\le M\}}]$. This is centered, stationary and $m$-dependent, with $\|V_t\|\le2M$. Put $\eta_{m,M}=\|Y_0-V_0\|_{L^2(H)}$. Since $EY_0=0$, $\eta_{m,M}\le2\|Y_0\mathbf1_{\{\|Y_0\|>M\}}\|_{L^2(H)}\to0$ by dominated convergence. The centered residual $Y-V$ is $m$-dependent, so its covariances vanish at distances greater than $m$ and all remaining scalar covariances have absolute value at most $\eta_{m,M}^2$. Hence its normalized weighted block has second moment at most $A^2(2m+1)\eta_{m,M}^2$. With $Z^V_{j,b}=b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^bc_{b,\ell}V_{j+\ell-1}$, step 2.1 and Minkowski give $\sup_{j,b}\|Z_{j,b}-Z^V_{j,b}\|_{L^2(H)}\le d_{m,M}:=A\varepsilon_m+A\sqrt{2m+1}\eta_{m,M}$. Choose first $m$ and then $M$ to make this arbitrarily small.

For independent centered Hilbert elements $U_1,\ldots,U_q$ bounded by $L$, write $\|\sum_iU_i\|^2=\sum_i\|U_i\|^2+2\sum_{i<j}\langle U_i,U_j\rangle$. On squaring, every term containing an index exactly once has expectation zero, by integrating that independent centered element first. In particular all mixed terms between the two sums vanish; among products of two inner products only identical pairs survive. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives $E\|\sum_iU_i\|^4\le\sum_iE\|U_i\|^4+6\sum_{i<j}E\|U_i\|^2E\|U_j\|^2\le3q^2L^4$; the empty sum is zero. Partition the $b$ summands defining $\sqrt b Z^V_{j,b}$ into $p=m+1$ residue classes. Inside each class their input innovation sets are disjoint, hence they are jointly independent. Applying the proved bound to the class sizes $q_s$ and using $\|\sum_{s=1}^pu_s\|^4\le p^3\sum_s\|u_s\|^4$ and $\sum_sq_s^2\le b^2$ gives $\sup_{j,b}E\|Z^V_{j,b}\|^4\le3p^3A^4(2M)^4=:C_{m,M}$. Thus fourth moments are used only for bounded truncations.

The rank-one identity and Cauchy–Schwarz imply both $\sup_{j,b}E|\|Z_{j,b}\|^2-\|Z^V_{j,b}\|^2|\le d_{m,M}(2A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})$ and $\sup_{j,b}E\|Z_{j,b}\otimes Z_{j,b}-Z^V_{j,b}\otimes Z^V_{j,b}\|_1\le d_{m,M}(2A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})$. Here use $\|Z_{j,b}\|_{L^2}\le A\sqrt K$ and $\|u\otimes u-v\otimes v\|_1\le\|u-v\|(\|u\|+\|v\|)$. The squared truncated blocks are uniformly integrable by step 3.1 and Markov's inequality. For nonnegative $F,G$, splitting at $G>L/2$ proves $E[F\mathbf1_{\{F>L\}}]\le2E|F-G|+E[G\mathbf1_{\{G>L/2\}}]$. Apply this with the two squared block norms, then let $L\to\infty$ and $d_{m,M}\to0$. This proves the asserted uniform integrability for $Z$.

Fix $m,M$ and set $Q_n^V=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NZ^V_{j,b}\otimes Z^V_{j,b}$ and $B_n=EQ_n^V$. For fixed unit vectors $e,f$, the real variables $\langle Z^V_{j,b},e\rangle\langle Z^V_{j,b},f\rangle$ have second moments at most $C_{m,M}$. When two starts differ by more than $b+m$, the blocks use disjoint original innovations and disjoint replacement arrays, so these variables are independent. Expanding the variance of their empirical mean therefore gives $E|\langle(Q_n^V-B_n)f,e\rangle|^2\le C_{m,M}(2(b+m)+1)/N\to0$, since $b/n\to0$. For any fixed finite-rank orthogonal projection $P$ of rank $d$, expansion in an orthonormal basis of its range and the rank-one norm bound show $\|P(Q_n^V-B_n)P\|_1\le\sum_{u,v\le d}|\langle(Q_n^V-B_n)e_v,e_u\rangle|$. Thus its expectation tends to zero.

Choose complete basis projections $P_d$ and put $R_d=I-P_d$. For any square-integrable $H$-valued $U$, the operator $T=E[U\otimes U]$ satisfies $\|T-PTP\|_1\le E\|RU\|^2+2\sqrt{E\|PU\|^2 E\|RU\|^2}$: expand its four $P,R$ corners, use the rank-one norm inequality on each off-diagonal corner, and use positivity for the $R$ corner. The same inequality holds for an empirical average, using its finite empirical expectation. For the $V$ blocks, finite dependence and covariance expansion give $E\|R_dZ^V_{j,b}\|^2\le A^2(2m+1)E\|R_dV_0\|^2=:t_d\to0$ by dominated convergence. Also $\sup_{j,b}E\|Z^V_{j,b}\|^2\le (A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})^2=:C$. Applying the corner inequality to $Q_n^V$ and $B_n$, and then Cauchy–Schwarz to expectations, yields $E\|Q_n^V-B_n\|_1\le E\|P_d(Q_n^V-B_n)P_d\|_1+2t_d+4\sqrt{Ct_d}$. Send $n\to\infty$ by step 4.1, then $d\to\infty$. This proves trace-norm concentration locally, without inferring trace-norm convergence from coordinate convergence alone.

Define $Q_n=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NZ_{j,b}\otimes Z_{j,b}$. By step 3.2, $E\|Q_n-Q_n^V\|_1$ and $\|EQ_n-B_n\|_1$ are each at most $d_{m,M}(2A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})$. The triangle inequality and step 4.2 therefore give $\limsup_n E\|Q_n-EQ_n\|_1\le2d_{m,M}(2A\sqrt K+d_{m,M})$. First send $M\to\infty$ for each fixed $m$, then send $m\to\infty$. It follows that $E\|Q_n-EQ_n\|_1\to0$. This concentration conclusion required only the uniform bound on weights.

Now impose the squared normalization and fixed-lag autocorrelation hypotheses. Extend each weight vector by zero. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|q_b(h)|\le1$. With $C_h=E[X_0\otimes X_h]$, stationarity gives $EQ_n=C_0+\sum_{h=1}^{b-1}q_b(h)(C_h+C_h^*)$. The series is absolutely convergent in trace norm by step 1.1. On each finite set of lags $q_b(h)\to1$, and the remaining trace-norm tail is uniformly bounded by its summable covariance tail. Thus $EQ_n\to\Gamma$ in trace norm. Step 4.3 gives $E\|Q_n-\Gamma\|_1\to0$. The empirically centered covariance equals $Q_n-\bar Z_{n,b}\otimes\bar Z_{n,b}$, whose difference from $Q_n$ has expected trace norm $E\|\bar Z_{n,b}\|^2\le A^2Kb/N\to0$ by step 1.2. This proves the asserted $L^1$ limit and its probability consequence by Markov's inequality.

MBB has $q_b(h)=(1-h/b)_+$ and squared normalization exactly. For TBB the squared normalization is also exact and the coefficients are bounded eventually by [F5]. Extend its nonnegative unimodal coefficients by zero to all integers; the total variation is at most $2A$. Telescoping gives $\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z}|c_{b,\ell+h}-c_{b,\ell}|\le2Ah$, so $|q_b(h)-q_b(0)|\le2A^2h/b\to0$. This uses exactly the midpoint coefficients of the algorithm and requires no continuity of the taper. All proved limits and uniform-integrability conclusions apply after any finite initial set of block sizes is discarded. The moment and projection conclusions, covariance limit, and claimed specializations are now established.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal Bernoulli shift in $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R)$ under [[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and suppose additionally that $m\delta_m\to0$. Put $\sigma=\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}$, let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator, and put

$$K=\sigma^2+2\sigma\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h.$$

For every integer $b\ge1$, let $c_{b,1},\ldots,c_{b,b}$ be deterministic real weights, uniformly bounded in absolute value by $A<\infty$. Define

$$Z_{j,b}=b^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=1}^b c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1}.$$

Then $\{\|Z_{j,b}\|_H^2:j\in\mathbb Z,b\ge1\}$ is uniformly integrable, and for $0\le q\le b$,

$$E\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}X_{j+\ell-1}\right\|_H^2\le A^2Kq.$$

If $P$ is any finite-rank orthogonal projection, $R=I-P$ and $\alpha_P=\|RX_0\|_{L^2(H)}$, then also

$$E\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^q c_{b,\ell}RX_{j+\ell-1}\right\|_H^2\le A^2q\left(\alpha_P^2+2\alpha_P\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h\right).$$

For $n\ge b$, set $N=n-b+1$ and $\bar Z_{n,b}=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^NZ_{j,b}$. Then

$$E\|\bar Z_{n,b}\|_H^2\le A^2Kb/N.$$

Suppose further that $b=b_n\to\infty$, $b_n/n\to0$, and the weights satisfy

$$b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^bc_{b,\ell}^2=1,\qquad q_b(h):=b^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{b-h}c_{b,\ell}c_{b,\ell+h}\longrightarrow1\quad\text{for every fixed }h\ge0.$$

The centered overlapping-block covariance then satisfies the stronger $L^1$ trace-norm limit

$$E\left\|N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N(Z_{j,b}-\bar Z_{n,b})\otimes(Z_{j,b}-\bar Z_{n,b})-\Gamma\right\|_1\longrightarrow0.$$

In particular it converges in probability in trace norm. Both the MBB weights $c_{b,\ell}=1$ and the actual TBB weights $c_{b,\ell}=a_bw((\ell-\tfrac12)/b)$ satisfy these weight hypotheses for all sufficiently large $b$. For any complete finite or countable orthonormal basis and its initial-coordinate projections $P_d$, the projection-tail coefficient $\alpha_{P_d}^2+2\alpha_{P_d}\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h$ tends to zero as $d\to\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered
$H$-valued Gaussian random element with covariance $\Gamma$, whose existence
is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$
in the weak topology of Borel probability measures on $H$. The covariance
kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a
compact self-adjoint operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Then $T$ has a
Hilbert basis ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]])
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]): one may take the union
of orthonormal bases of the finitely many-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces with a
Hilbert basis of $\ker T$. If $\ker T=\{0\}$ no vectors from the kernel are
needed, and if all nonzero eigenspaces are absent (that is $T=0$) the union is a
Hilbert basis of $H=\ker T$.

If $\mathbb EX=0$ and $\mathbb EX^2=\sigma^2<\infty$, then $\varphi_X(t)=1-\sigma^2t^2/2+o(t^2)$ as $t\to0$. No third moment or choice axiom is assumed. The same scalar estimates give $0\le1-\cos u\le u^2/2$ for every real u. More precisely, for $r(u)=e^{iu}-1-iu+u^2/2$, $$|r(u)|\le \min(|u|^3/3,4u^2),\qquad |e^{iu}-1-iu|\le u^2.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

$X_n\to X$ in probability if and only if every subsequence of $(X_n)$ has a
further subsequence converging almost surely to $X$.

If $X_n\to X$ in probability, then some subsequence $X_{n_k}$ converges to
$X$ almost surely.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $E$ be a separable complete metric space, let $\mathcal D_n$ be the sigma-algebra generated by the observed data at sample size $n$, and let $Z_n^*$ be a bootstrap random element whose remaining randomness is the resampling randomization. Write $\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*)$ for its conditional Borel probability law given $\mathcal D_n$. Choose a metric $d_w$ on Borel probability measures on $E$ such that $d_w(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$ exactly when $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ in the sense of [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. For a fixed Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $E$, we say that $Z_n^*$ converges conditionally weakly in probability to $\mu$ when

$$d_w\!\left(\mathcal L^*(Z_n^*),\mu\right)\longrightarrow 0\quad\hbox{in probability}.$$

We use this definition only on separable Hilbert spaces and their finite products.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

Throughout, $H$ and $K$ are real or complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-hilbert-space]]), $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) of
operator norm $\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]), and $E$ is a **Hilbert basis**
of $H$, that is, a complete orthonormal subset of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
The basis $E$ is **supplied as data**; the definitions below are stated
relative to it.

**The Hilbert–Schmidt square-sum.** The family $(\|Te\|^2)_{e\in E}$ consists of
nonnegative real numbers and is indexed by the arbitrary set $E$. Its sum is the
supremum of the finite subsums,

$$s_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2 \;:\; F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

in the finite-subset-supremum convention of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]; the empty finite
subset contributes the empty sum $0$, so the supremum is over a nonempty
set and exists in $[0,+\infty]$. No enumeration, ordering or countability of
$E$ is used or asserted, and no choice is performed: the supremum ranges over
the set of finite subsets of the fixed index set $E$. For finite $E$ the
supremum is the ordinary finite sum over $E$, because all terms are
nonnegative.

**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a basis.** The operator $T$ is
**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$** when $s_E(T)<+\infty$, that is, when the
finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$. In that case the
**Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ relative to $E$** is the nonnegative square root

$$\|T\|_{HS,E}:=\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,+\infty).$$

When $s_E(T)=+\infty$, no Hilbert–Schmidt norm relative to $E$ is defined, and
$T$ is not Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**Degenerate and extreme cases.** The zero operator satisfies $s_E(0)=0$ for
every basis $E$, so it is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every basis with norm
$0$. If $H=\{0\}$ then the empty family is a Hilbert basis of $H$, the only
finite subset is empty, and $s_\varnothing(T)=0$ for the only linear operator
$T:\{0\}\to K$; that operator is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to the empty basis
with norm $0$. If $H$ is finite dimensional and $E$ is finite, $s_E(T)$ is an
ordinary finite sum of the squared norms $\|Te\|^2$, and $T$ is automatically
Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**The basis is part of the notation.** The symbol $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ keeps the
basis in the subscript on purpose. Until the next result is proved, the phrase
"$T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt" is never used without a specified Hilbert basis, and
nothing here asserts that a Hilbert basis of $H$ exists: the existence of $E$
is a hypothesis of the definition, and the question of whether the finiteness
of $s_E(T)$ and the value $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ depend on $E$ is taken up in
[[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]. In particular this
definition makes no basis-existence claim and no comparison with the operator
norm $\|T\|$; every such statement is proved later, where its own hypotheses
are displayed.

**Notation.** For a finite $F\subseteq E$ we write
$s_F(T):=\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2$ for the finite subsum, so that
$s_E(T)=\sup\{s_F(T):F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\}$.

Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex inner-product
space $H$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and for $x\in H$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$Then: 1. $P_Fx$ lies in the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$, and $\|P_Fx\|^2=\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2$; 2. the residual $x-P_Fx$ is orthogonal to every $e_j$ with $j\in F$, hence to every vector of the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$; 3. $\|x-P_Fx\|^2=\|x\|^2-\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2$, and therefore the **finite Bessel inequality** holds:$$\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2\le\|x\|^2 ;$$4. $P_Fx$ is the unique best approximation to $x$ from the span of $\{e_i : i\in F\}$: for every $y$ in that span,$$\|x-y\|^2=\|x-P_Fx\|^2+\|P_Fx-y\|^2\ge\|x-P_Fx\|^2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if $y=P_Fx$.

At $F=\varnothing$ the sum defining $P_Fx$ is empty, so $P_Fx=0$ and the
identities read $\|x\|^2=\|x\|^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First, for a nuclear representation $T=\sum_j\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j$ and an orthogonal projection $R$, its absolutely convergent trace has $|\operatorname{tr}(RTR)|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|$. For every finite orthonormal set $E$, Minkowski and Bessel give $(\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2)^{1/2}\le\sum_j\|v_j\|(\sum_{e\in E}|\langle e,u_j\rangle|^2)^{1/2}\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|$. Infinite nuclear sums follow from their summable tails. Taking the nuclear infimum proves $|\operatorname{tr}(RTR)|\le\|T\|_1$ and $\|T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|T\|_1$ by [F5]. Subtraction of $M_n$ replaces $B_{j,q}$ by $B_{j,q}-s_qM_n$, where $s_q=\sum_{\ell=1}^qc_{b,\ell}$ does not depend on $j$. It changes $\bar B_q$ by exactly the same amount. Thus every centered block is unchanged. Independence of the starts gives $\operatorname{Cov}^*(Z_n^*)=(kC_b+C_r)/n$. Positivity and the rank-one trace formula give $E\operatorname{tr}C_r\le E\|B_{1,r}\|^2\le Dr$, so $E\|C_r/n\|_1\le Db/n\to0$. Since $kb/n\to1$, [F1] now gives the asserted trace-norm covariance limit. The conditional squared norm of the centered remainder has expectation $\operatorname{tr}(C_r/n)$ and therefore its unconditional expectation tends to zero at rate $O(b/n)$.

Set $U_j=B_{j,b}/\sqrt b$, $\bar U=\bar B_b/\sqrt b$, and $V_j=U_j-\bar U$. For any vectors $x,y$ and $a>0$, splitting according as the larger summand exceeds $a/2$ gives $\|x+y\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|x+y\|>a\}}\le4\|x\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|x\|>a/2\}}+4\|y\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|y\|>a/2\}}$. Consequently, for each $\varepsilon>0$, the conditional Lindeberg sum of the $k$ complete blocks is at most
$$L_n(\varepsilon)=\frac{kb}{nN}\sum_{j=1}^N\|V_j\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|V_j\|>\varepsilon\sqrt{n/b}\}},\qquad E L_n(\varepsilon)\le4E\!\left[\|U_1\|^2\mathbf1_{\{\|U_1\|>(\varepsilon/2)\sqrt{n/b}\}}\right]+4E\|\bar U\|^2\longrightarrow0.$$
Here $n/b\to\infty$, stationarity makes the expected empirical uncentered tail equal to that of $U_1$, and [F1] supplies uniform integrability and $E\|\bar U\|^2\to0$. Hence $L_n(\varepsilon)\to0$ in probability by [F5].

Take any subsequence. Apply [F4] diagonally to the scalar trace-norm covariance error, $\operatorname{tr}(C_r/n)$, and $L_n(1/j)$ for positive integers $j$. There is a further subsequence on which all tend to zero almost surely. Fix a data outcome in this probability-one event. For any $a\in H$, let $\xi_n=\langle a,B_{J_1,b}-\bar B_b\rangle/\sqrt n$ and $v_n=kE^*\xi_n^2$. Step 1.1 and remainder negligibility give $v_n\to\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle$, and the norm Lindeberg bounds imply $kE^*[\xi_n^2\mathbf1_{\{|\xi_n|>\rho\}}]\to0$ for every $\rho>0$. The Taylor bound in [F3], split at $\rho$, gives
$$k\left|E^*e^{i\xi_n}-1+\tfrac12E^*\xi_n^2\right|\le (\rho/3)v_n+4kE^*[\xi_n^2\mathbf1_{\{|\xi_n|>\rho\}}].$$
Let $n\to\infty$ and then $\rho\downarrow0$. Thus $k(E^*e^{i\xi_n}-1)\to-\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle/2$ and $k|E^*e^{i\xi_n}-1|^2\to0$, since $k\to\infty$. The convergent power-series expansion $\log(1+z)=z+O(|z|^2)$ near zero proves $(E^*e^{i\xi_n})^k\to\exp(-\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle/2)$. The remainder's characteristic function tends to one by Cauchy--Schwarz and step 1.1. Replacing $a$ by $ta$ covers every real frequency. Therefore [F3] gives weak convergence of every finite-dimensional projection of the conditional law to that of $G$, on this fixed outcome; no positive lower bound on any variance was used.

On the same outcome let $T_n=\operatorname{Cov}^*(Z_n^*)$. For every fixed $d$, conditional centering and [F5] give $E^*\|R_dZ_n^*\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(R_dT_nR_d)\to\operatorname{tr}(R_d\Gamma R_d)$. If $\phi$ is bounded uniformly continuous, put $M=\sup|\phi|$ and $\omega_\phi(h)=\sup_{\|x-y\|\le h}|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|$. Markov gives
$$|E^*\phi(Z_n^*)-E^*\phi(P_dZ_n^*)|\le\omega_\phi(h)+2Mh^{-2}\operatorname{tr}(R_dT_nR_d).$$
The analogous bound for $G$ uses $\operatorname{tr}(R_d\Gamma R_d)$. Step 3.1 gives convergence of the projected expectations. Take the limit superior in $n$, then $d\to\infty$, and finally $h\downarrow0$. All such test expectations converge, so [F4] gives weak convergence of the full conditional laws on this outcome. Thus their distance to the law of $G$ in the metric of [F4] tends to zero almost surely on the extracted subsequence. The subsequence characterization proves convergence in probability along the original sequence.

To verify tightness explicitly, empirical centering decreases each projected second moment. By [F1] and independence,
$$E E^*\|R_dZ_n^*\|^2\le\frac{k b+r}{n}D_d=D_d.$$
The same bound without projection is $D$. Enlarge constants to cover any finitely many initial admissible block lengths. Given $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, choose $R$ and increasing integers $d_j$ so that $D/R^2<\varepsilon\eta/4$ and $j^2D_{d_j}<\varepsilon\eta\,2^{-j-2}$. The closed set
$$K=\{x\in H:\|x\|\le R,\ \|R_{d_j}x\|\le1/j\text{ for every }j\ge1\}$$
is compact: for any radius choose $j$ with $1/j$ smaller than half the radius, and a finite net for the bounded ball in $P_{d_j}H$; this gives a finite net for $K$, and closedness in complete $H$ gives compactness. Markov and the union bound yield $E P^*(Z_n^*\notin K)<\varepsilon\eta/2$, and then $P\{P^*(Z_n^*\notin K)>\varepsilon\}<\eta/2$. This proves the stated conditional tightness, and steps 1.1-4.1 establish all the other assertions.

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes positive sample and block lengths and b tending to infinity; an empty process or empty asymptotic sequence is outside its domain.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 3.1 include zero covariance; characteristic functions converge to one and no variance is divided out.
